title: Quality and reliability of YouTube videos in Arabic as a source of patient information on prostate cancer
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of 100 Arabic-language YouTube videos on prostate cancer in which every video was assigned to one of four content categories (useful, misleading, personal experience, irrelevant); the share coded 'misleading' is a quantitative share of classified items with a stated denominator (100 videos), i.e. a CONTENT prevalence estimate. The GQS and modified DISCERN instruments are quality/reliability scales and are reported only as medians (plus speaker subgroup distributions), so they yield no overall share.

estimates.country: Arabic-language videos; upload location recorded, most content from Egypt (24%)
estimates.measure_type: % of Arabic-language prostate-cancer YouTube videos whose content was labelled misleading
estimates.denominator: 100 Arabic-language YouTube videos on prostate cancer retrieved with three Arabic keyword terms under YouTube's default relevance sort
estimates.definition: Video assigned to the 'misleading' category of a four-way content classification (useful, misleading, personal experience, irrelevant) by the study team; explicit criteria for the misleading category are not reported
estimates.misinfo_def: "Retrieved videos were analysed and categorised into four groups according to content as useful, misleading, personal experience, or irrelevant." (no formal definition of misinformation is given; 'misinformation' appears as a keyword and in the analysis heading 'quality analysis and misinformation tools')
estimates.source_quote: The video content was labeled as useful in 84% of videos, misleading in 6%, irrelevant in 6%, and depicted personal experience in 4% of videos.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors' own categorisation of video content into four groups; number of raters, coding rubric and inter-rater reliability are not reported. GQS (5-point Likert) and modified DISCERN (5 points) were applied to the useful videos only.
estimates.moderator_quote: The terms in Arabic (Prostate cancer, prostate cancer treatment and prostate) were used to search YouTube (www.YouTube.com) (Supplementary Table 1). The default search setting on YouTube was used, which automatically sorts videos by relevance. ... A total of 100 videos were collected, over 4 months (26.06.2022-27.10.2022) during the searches for the search terms and were compiled into a playlist for evaluation.
estimates.notes: borderline=true because the four-way scheme mixes veracity ('misleading') with relevance/genre categories ('irrelevant', 'personal experience') and no rubric or reliability statistic is given, so the 6% rests on unspecified researcher judgement. Note an internal inconsistency in the paper: the abstract states '86% were found to have useful content, while 14% were found to be misleading or irrelevant', whereas the Results give 84% useful / 6% misleading / 6% irrelevant / 4% personal experience. The Results figures (which separate misleading from irrelevant) are used here; the abstract's 14% pools misleading with irrelevant and so is not a misinformation share. Country coding: sampling was by language, not country; the paper reports upload locations only as 'most of the content created was from Egypt (24%)', so nations are not fully enumerated - coded Multi-country/multi for the Arab world rather than Global.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the abstract's '14% were found to be misleading or irrelevant' - it pools the misleading category with 'irrelevant' videos, which are off-topic rather than false, so it is not a misinformation share (and it contradicts the Results). (2) GQS and modified DISCERN results - QUALITY instruments, and the only overall figures are medians ('The median GQS score of the useful videos was 4 (IQR: 4-5), while the median modified DISCERN tool was 4 (IQR: 3-4)'), i.e. scale scores with no share of items, so no row. (3) Table 3's category shares (e.g. 'higher moderate to excellent levels of quality (80.5% versus 21.7%)') are QUALITY and are speaker-type subgroups, not the paper's headline prevalence. (4) 'A significant proportion of 78% of low-reliability videos (<=2) was presented by non-health workers' is a share OF low-reliability videos that came from non-health workers, not a share of videos that were low-reliability - wrong denominator, unusable. Summing DISCERN<=2 cells across Table 3 (5/77 + 18/23) would be a cross-category sum, forbidden by R8. (5) Discussion figures '92% were deemed useful' / '78% had low reliability, and only 56% were deemed useful' are speaker subgroups of a usefulness rating, and the 92%/56% cannot be reconciled with Table 2/3 as printed. (6) Third-party figures quoted from Steinberg et al (73% fair or poor) and Loeb et al (77% potentially misinformative) are cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis; three Arabic keyword searches under default relevance sorting over 26.06.2022-27.10.2022; 110 videos retrieved, 10 excluded (7 non-Arabic, 3 duplicates), 100 analysed; videos categorised into four content groups by the authors and useful videos scored with GQS and modified DISCERN; no number of coders, no coding manual and no inter-rater reliability reported; no response-rate concept (content study); analysis limited to descriptive statistics with t-test/Mann-Whitney comparisons by speaker type.
rob.item6_quote: Retrieved videos were analysed and categorised into four groups according to content as useful, misleading, personal experience, or irrelevant.
rob.item10_quote: The video content was labeled as useful in 84% of videos, misleading in 6%, irrelevant in 6%, and depicted personal experience in 4% of videos.
